articles.title: AIM-260 JATM Missile Spotted On Australian Super Hornet
articles.text:
A Royal Australian Air Force F/A-18F Super Hornet has been photographed carrying an inert AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile (JATM) during a major U.S. Navy test event in California. The development comes weeks after Australia announced that it would buy the new missile, with its Super Hornets being the first RAAF aircraft to receive it.

The photograph was released by the U.S. Navy and shows an RAAF F/A-18F assigned to No. 1 Squadron taking off from Naval Base Ventura County Point Mugu on September 11 during Gray Flag 2026. The loadout also includes a CATM-9X — the inert training variant of the AIM-9X — and a CATM-120, the inert training version of the AIM-120 AMRAAM, three external fuel tanks, an AN/ASQ-228 ATFLIR targeting pod, and a Tactical Combat Training System (TCTS) pod.

Gray Flag is the naval aviation test community’s flagship large-force test event, providing opportunities for large-scale integration of new capabilities across services, platforms, industry, and allied forces. Gray Flag 2026 was the largest edition of the exercise to date. According to the Navy, more than 3,000 personnel from over 150 organizations participated, flying more than 750 sorties and logging over 2,000 flight hours across hundreds of multi-domain test objectives.

Previous iterations of Gray Flag have been used to test new and still-developmental weapons in increasingly complex, operationally representative scenarios, including actual missile engagements against realistic targets. Making use of the sprawling Point Mugu Sea Range, the event has also become an important opportunity for working out how sensors, weapons, aircraft, and networks interact as part of larger kill chains and kill webs. A new, longer-range air-to-air missile is especially relevant when it comes to developing tactics, techniques, and procedures within a broader, networked air-combat architecture.

Beyond being the first apparent glimpse of an Australian JATM in any context, integration of the weapon onto Australia’s Super Hornet fleet has already progressed to the point of carrying the missile — in inert form — during a major U.S.-based test and integration exercise.

As TWZ reported in August, Australia is set to become the first country outside the United States to operate the AIM-260 following a roughly $480-million procurement through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales program. The Australian government said at the time that the missile would first be integrated onto the RAAF’s F/A-18F fleet, before being fielded on the F-35A and EA-18G Growler. Looking further ahead, the RAAF’s MQ-28 Ghost Bat collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) could also emerge as a candidate for integration with JATM.

Australia’s announcement did not provide a delivery schedule or specify when JATM would enter Australian service.

The overall proportions and external configuration of the AIM-260 were revealed when an example appeared on a U.S. Navy F/A-18F in May of this year. That aircraft, operated by Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 31 (VX-31), provided the first publicly known photographic view of the highly classified missile.

The AIM-260’s exact specifications remain classified. It is intended to provide substantially greater range than the AIM-120 AMRAAM while retaining a broadly similar form factor. That compact configuration is important because the missile is designed not only for external carriage but also for internal carriage by aircraft such as the F-22 and F-35.

The weapon has been developed as a response to the increasingly long-range air-to-air threat posed by China’s PL-15 and other advanced missiles. Official range figures have not been released, although previous reporting has pointed to an intended range of at least 120 miles and potentially considerably more.

The Australian procurement therefore represents an important expansion of the JATM program beyond the U.S. fleet.

The timing of the Point Mugu photograph is particularly interesting. Gray Flag is specifically intended to bring together large numbers of aircraft, weapons, sensors, networks, and other systems for demanding integration and test activities. An Australian Super Hornet carrying JATM at such an event would be entirely in line with the purpose of the exercise.

It is not clear, however, what role the missile was playing. The photograph does not establish whether it was an Australian-owned operational weapon, a U.S. test asset, or a missile being used for a particular integration activity. Blue bands on the missile body confirm that it’s a training missile with inert rocket motor and/or warhead.

Public evidence of an Australian aircraft carrying the AIM-260 is another important milestone in the weapon’s transition from a closely guarded U.S. development program toward allied service.

It also underscores the most interoperability aspect of the Australian acquisition. Canberra is buying into a U.S. long-range air-to-air weapon program at a time when the Royal Australian Air Force and U.S. forces are increasingly expected to operate together across the Indo-Pacific.

The exercise also comes as the U.S. moves to accelerate development and future production of the AIM-260. In September, the Pentagon and Lockheed Martin reached a framework agreement laying the groundwork for a future multiyear procurement deal, while the Air Force Test Center confirmed that the missile is already undergoing both ground and airborne testing. The agreement is intended to give Lockheed Martin and its suppliers the demand signal needed to expand production capacity, although the number of missiles, costs and delivery schedule remain undisclosed.

The development should also be seen in the context of broader U.S.-Australian cooperation on air-launched weapons. RAAF F/A-18Fs are also being integrated into the U.S.-Australian Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) effort under the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment (SCIFiRE), with Australia providing test infrastructure for the weapon’s flight-test program. You can read more about this program here.

The video below shows a hypersonic test conducted at Woomera in 2016 under the U.S.-Australian Hypersonic International Flight Research Experimentation (HiFIRE) program.

Australia said its F/A-18Fs would be the first RAAF aircraft to receive JATM, and an Australian Super Hornet has now been photographed carrying one during a major U.S. Navy test event. For the RAAF, getting JATM onto its frontline fighters is consequently an increasingly urgent requirement, giving its Super Hornets a credible long-range counter to the weapons they could face in a future high-end fight.

Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com

articles.title: Suspected Chinese spies spoofed an Anthropic exec, ex-White House official in AI phishing
articles.text: A suspected Chinese espionage group impersonated AI policy figures, including a senior Anthropic employee and a former White House official, in phishing campaigns targeting AI policy experts at US universities, think tanks, and law firms, security researchers say. The bulk of these campaigns occurred in July, according to Proofpoint, which discovered the espionage attempts and attributed them to a China-aligned group it tracks as TA419. Proofpoint’s security alert comes a day after OpenAI accused China’s Moonshot AI of stealing the American models’ reasoning and other data in distillation attacks that began on July 1. “In July 2026, TA419 impersonated multiple individuals, including a former member of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy leadership team, in credential phishing campaigns targeting AI policy experts in the US,” Proofpoint threat-intelligence analyst Mark Kelly said in a Thursday report. Beginning July 8, TA419 sent phishing emails spoofing Lynne Edwards Parker, the former principal deputy director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, and then Heidi Crebo-Rediker, a prominent economist and foreign policy expert, to even more American AI policy experts at think tanks, universities, and law firms. The suspected spies’ emails invited their targets to join a fake AI policy advisory committee or contribute to a Senate foreign relations committee report on AI export controls and supply chains. If the American AI expert replied, the Beijing-linked crew responded with a shortened URL promising to share additional details, but in reality pointing to an attacker-controlled domain. This page conducts a Cloudflare Turnstile check behind a phony OneDrive loading screen, and then redirects the victim to an attacker-in-the-middle (AitM) credential phishing page that steals the victim’s cloud account login information. The July 2026 campaigns used driftshare[.]co as the first-stage domain and globalfileshareplatform[.]com as the second-stage domain. In February - as US military officials pressured Anthropic to remove Claude’s safeguards - the Chinese spies spoofed a senior Anthropic employee to phish an AI policy analyst at a US think tank. This email used the subject line: “Request for Feedback on Military Integration of Claude.” TA419’s phishing chain targets Microsoft 365/Entra ID through the first-party OfficeHome application (client_id=4765445b-32c6-49b0-83e6-1d93765276ca). It’s built on open source Frameless BitB, which contains a Browser-in-the-Browser (BitB) overlay, an Evilginx phishlet to intercept usernames, passwords, and session cookies for Microsoft 365, and server-side substitution rules that inject the kit into proxied pages. TA419 typically uses Cloudflare’s content delivery network to hide the backend hosting IP address for its domains, and its credential phishing domains are usually themed around file sharing sites and cloud services - such as msfile[.]online and onecloudfilesync[.]com. It also impersonates specific organizations, including the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association (tw-koryu[.]org), The Heritage Foundation (heritiages[.]org and heritiage[.]org), and Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjirō Koizumi’s official website (shinjirou[.]info). In total, the crew uses dozens of phishing and spoofed-sender domains, and phony email addresses. Proofpoint includes all of the ones it discovered in 2026, plus the timeline of when they were registered or first seen, so check out those indicators, too. TA419 and other Beijing-aligned crews will likely continue targeting AI and other policy experts working on technologies of interest to the Chinese government, according to the threat hunters. “Organizations in the scope of TA419 activity should consider phishing-resistant, origin-bound authentication such as passkeys,” they recommend.®

articles.title: With most information hidden, the game Stratego
articles.text:
Deep Blue took down Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, and poker bots have been beating professionals for years. But one classic game called Stratego held out. Even DeepMind, with its exceptional budget, couldn't build a machine that reliably beat the best human players.

Now, a team of researchers from Carnegie Mellon, MIT, New York University, and Stanford University has done it. Their AI, called Ataraxos, beat Pim Niemeijer, arguably the best Stratego player of all time, 15 games to one, with four draws. And it took just 16 GPUs and a few thousand dollars to train it.

Hidden armies

In Stratego, each player gets 40 pieces representing military ranks, from a marshal down to a spy, plus bombs and a flag. You win by capturing the opponent's flag. Your opponent knows where your pieces are, but not what they are. Identities are revealed only when two pieces collide in battle—the weaker one is removed, and the identity of the winner is revealed. That makes Stratego an imperfect-information game, just like poker, which computers cracked years ago. “There's something super distinctive about Stratego, which is that it is a massive amount of hidden information that unfolds over a very long time scale,” said Eugene Vinitsky, a researcher at NYU and co-author of the study.

articles.title: X-BAT Strengthens US Presence With Expansion Into Two Aerospace Hubs
articles.text:
Shield AI today named the two sites that will build and test X-BAT, its AI-piloted fighter jet designed to take off and land vertically. X-Forge 2, at the Newton City-County Airport in Kansas, is the flight test and sustainment home for the aircraft. X-Forge 3, based in Des Moines, Washington, just south of Seattle, is the production home. Together with X-Forge 1 in Frisco, Texas, the three sites carry X-BAT from prototype through delivery and through the life of the fleet.
Every X-BAT will complete production acceptance testing in Newton before delivery, and customers will conduct their own acceptance flights there. Newton will also support development flight testing and serve as the center for maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) for the fleet. Shield AI currently leases hangar and office space and approximately 10 acres at Newton City/County Airport and is working with the City of Newton and Harvey County to expand its footprint and develop a larger hangar.
South-central Kansas has built aircraft since the 1920s, and its training pipeline runs through Wichita State University, WSU Tech, the National Center for Aviation Training and Hutchinson Community College. Shield AI committed to Newton in 2025, when it first showed the X-BAT design to the public, and has been standing the site up since.
In Des Moines, Shield AI has signed its lease and is building the site out now. Hiring for the program has shifted to the region and is underway. Des Moines is the company’s first Puget Sound site, and Shield AI expects its footprint in the region to grow as production rates climb. King County has more than 45,000 aerospace workers at more than 400 companies, and Washington’s supplier base runs past 1,500 firms. Shield AI evaluated several regions and chose Washington for that workforce.
“Both these regions were building airplanes before Shield AI existed, and we went to them for that reason,” said Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft at Shield AI. “Wichita’s track record speaks for itself, with more than a hundred years of aircraft manufacturing and more than a third of all American general aviation airplanes built there. Flight test is where an airplane earns its way, and Kansas has the airspace, the hangars and the people who have spent their careers around airplanes. Puget Sound has been producing aircraft at rate for seventy years and has the engineers, technicians and suppliers that takes. X-BAT will be built in Washington and fly in Kansas before it goes to a customer, and Kansas will keep this fleet in the air for decades.”
X-BAT is planned to begin production in 2029 and reaches full rate in the early 2030s. An economic analysis of the program estimates what each region gains if it runs as planned, and the employment projections reflect the program at rate. In the Newton area, X-BAT supports about 1,800 jobs in the early 2030s and about 2,900 by 2046, adding roughly $5 billion to the regional economy over that period. In the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue region, it supports about 8,000 jobs in the early 2030s and about 27,000 by 2046, adding roughly $73 billion. The counts include people employed by Shield AI, people at suppliers, and the jobs that local spending by both groups sustains.
Frisco, Texas remains Shield AI’s prototyping site and the home of V-BAT, and the company continues to build, operate and hire there. The analysis puts Frisco alone at about 600 jobs in the early 2030s and about 700 by 2046. Texas suppliers carry much of the rest of the program, including propulsion and mission systems work. Across the state, X-BAT is projected to support about 1,400 jobs in the early 2030s and about 7,900 by 2046, adding roughly $18.6 billion to the Texas economy.
Additional Quotes
Kansas
“Shield AI’s decision to base maintenance, repair and overhaul and sustainment operations for its X-BAT aircraft in Newton is great news for our state,” said Senator Jerry Moran. “Keeping advanced aircraft mission-ready is critical to our national security, and Kansas’ long history in aviation makes our state a natural home for this work. Our aviation workforce and training institutions are ready to support this mission. I am confident this partnership will grow in the years ahead as we help make certain our warfighters have the capabilities they need, when they need them.”
“Kansans have been building and flying airplanes for more than a hundred years, and Shield AI came to Newton because nobody does it better,” said Senator Roger Marshall. “Every U.S.-built X-BAT will earn its wings in Kansas skies before it is delivered to a customer, and thousands of Kansas workers will help keep the fleet flying for decades. That’s good news for our workforce and for our warfighters.”
“As the representative of the Air Capital of the World, I take great pride in the Kansans who have been building and flying airplanes for more than a century,” said Congressman Ron Estes. “Shield AI chose Newton as the flight test and sustainment home for X-BAT because of that experience. Every X-BAT will fly in Kansas before it goes into service, and the work to keep this fleet flying will happen here for years to come. Expanding their presence in Newton means good-paying jobs for Kansans and a lasting role for our state in America’s national security. I look forward to seeing this program continue to grow in Kansas.”
“Shield AI’s decision to make Newton the flight test and sustainment home for X-BAT reinforces our state’s leadership in aerospace,” Lieutenant Governor and Secretary of Commerce David Toland said. “Every X-BAT aircraft will be tested in Kansas before delivery, and our state’s aviation expertise will help keep the fleet flying for decades to come. From development through long-term operations, Kansas will play a critical role in the success of this next generation of American aerospace technology.”
“We are proud that Shield AI chose Newton in 2025 for the X-BAT flight test facility, and we are excited that our role has expanded to include the ongoing maintenance, repair and overhaul functions for the entire X-BAT fleet,” Mayor Rich Stinnett said. “It shows Newton has the talent, land and room to grow. Every X-BAT will prove itself here before it goes to a customer, and the work to keep the fleet flying will stay here for decades. That means long-term aviation jobs for Newton families. We look forward to a strong partnership as Shield AI continues its trajectory of incredible growth and innovation.”
Washington
“Washington has always been a place where big ideas take flight,” said Governor Bob Ferguson. “Our state brings together a world-leading aerospace industry, cutting-edge technology, and one of the most talented workforces anywhere in the world. Shield AI’s decision to build its new X-BAT manufacturing facility here is another sign that the future of aerospace is being built in Washington. We welcome Shield AI and the thousands of good-paying jobs this investment will bring.”
“King County continues to grow as a center for innovation and economic opportunity, and I look forward to welcoming Shield AI’s new X-BAT manufacturing facility in Des Moines,” said Congressman Adam Smith. “This hub will create high-quality jobs, strengthen Puget Sound’s expanding technology and aerospace sectors, and further diversify our local economy. Reimagining aviation will have a rightful home here in Washington’s Ninth District.”
“I want to welcome Shield AI to our community as we take these first few steps together,” said Yoshiko Grace Matsui, mayor of Des Moines, Washington. “Des Moines has long been home to families contributing to aerospace technology and operations. We are uniquely positioned to support a talented workforce in a new, burgeoning aerospace sector. Building a thriving business environment benefits all who live, work, and visit Des Moines.”
About X-BAT
X-BAT is designed as a long-range, survivable, AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, so it can operate from ships, islands or remote sites without a runway. It will carry weapons up to the 2,000-pound class in internal bays comparable in size to the F-35’s, have an objective combat radius of 1,000 nautical miles and support power-intensive electronic warfare and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance payloads. Powered by GE Aerospace’s F110 engine, X-BAT will fly on Shield AI’s Hivemind autonomy software, which enables operations without GPS or communications. Flight testing will begin later this year.

AWS offers local, open source leash for agent harnesses
articles.text: If you don't want your AI agents running out of control and changing files or transferring data outside your rules, AWS has published an open source software library that it claims can add a new layer of policy control. Just as a dog’s harness is useless without a leash to keep it under control, the Dogwood Local Engine promises to put AI agent tool calls on a leash, blocking actions that don’t meet user-defined temporal conditions. The DLE comes in the form of a Rust library that can be embedded into an agent’s harness or gateway and, to boil a long explanation down to a single sentence, simply issues allow/deny verdicts each time an agent tries to make a tool call. DLE doesn’t do the enforcement itself, AWS explained in its announcement writeup - that’s up to the harness itself - but it does check each tool call against policies defined using Dogwood, the open source governance language that AWS published in August. When AWS introduced Dogwood, it open sourced the language and reference tooling and added support for it to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore; DLE’s release makes the policy engine directly embeddable into agent harnesses. A key feature of both DLE and Dogwood is their awareness of temporal conditions. DLE tracks agent tool call events over time, stamping them into a log step by step. Those logs are persisted to a disk as each entry is made, allowing DLE to retain its state even if the entire system crashes or is restarted. The persistence step happens before DLE evaluates the applicable policy, and at the end of that process it returns a result: allow the action, or deny it, based on what the engine’s policies state. AWS gives the example of controlling coding agent Git pushes using DLE, defining a policy that only allows a push when the most recent test run has passed, and requiring that pass to have occurred within the past 15 minutes. If that’s not the case, the push is denied. “To accurately handle verdict enforcement, the harness intercepts every tool call, submits a request event to the engine, and runs the tool only if the engine’s verdict is allow,” AWS explained. This naturally raises the question of how much of a delay DLE introduces into agentic workflows; AWS claims the added delay is minimal. In tests simulating sessions from five minutes to 12 hours, DLE evaluation time was around 20 microseconds with a 15-minute window at the 12-hour mark, rising to about six milliseconds with a 24-hour window. DLE is also designed to prevent concurrent submission collisions by relying on a lock that only allows one event submission at a time, and that lock persists until policy evaluation is complete. AWS didn’t make clear from its writeup how that would handle a situation where, say, two concurrent submissions were made in which one fulfilled pass conditions and one caused a failure. We asked how incorrect enforcement could be prevented in those situations, but didn’t hear back prior to publication. Given repeated revelations of late that AI agents appear to regularly go off the (safety) rails imposed on them by human operators, the question of how durable DLE is also merits discussion. AWS admits that such situations are part of its reason for publishing the new library. “Left unchecked … tool calls can have irreparable consequences,” the DLE announcement concludes. “As agents scale to settings where they work autonomously for longer intervals with more tools, we need safeguards that can regulate how those tools are used.” AI agents finding holes in Dogwood and the DLE is likely a matter of time. Until then, feel free to give Dogwood and DLE a shot through its GitHub page. ®

articles.title: U.S. Mimics “Decoupled” Nuclear Detonation By Blowing Up A Tunnel Conventionally
articles.text:
The U.S. government set off conventional explosives inside a tunnel deep in the Nevada desert this week in a test designed to replicate a so-called “decoupled” nuclear detonation. Data collected is now being used to help improve methods for detecting this kind of nuclear testing. Just earlier this year, American authorities accused China of using decoupling to conceal new nuclear tests despite the country’s stated moratorium on such activities.

The test, which involved the use of chemical high-explosives and radiotracers, was conducted yesterday inside P Tunnel in Area 12 of the Nevada National Security Site (NNSA), according to a press release from the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA). The NNSS, which is situated within the boundaries of the U.S. Air Force’s Nevada Test and Training Range (NTTR), is used for a wide variety of testing purposes today. An agency under the Department of Energy, NNSA’s main jobs are to oversee the development and production of nuclear weapons, as well as manage America’s nuclear deterrent stockpile.

“This experiment is especially focused on further enhancing the U.S. capabilities to detect a ‘decoupled’ explosion,” per NNSA’s release. “Data collected from the experiment will be used to validate scientific models and refine algorithms that are critical to U.S. nuclear explosion detection efforts.”

“Just as a stealth aircraft looks smaller on radar, decoupling can greatly muffle the signals detected by nuclear detection sensors, making a large explosion appear smaller,” the release explains. “In a conventional, or ‘coupled,’ underground nuclear test, a device is placed deep in a hole in close contact with the rock, allowing much of the explosion’s shockwave to reach sensors. In a decoupled test, by contrast, the device is detonated inside a large underground chamber, substantially reducing the explosion’s seismic signature.”

“In this experiment, researchers gathered measurements using a broad suite of advanced sensors, including accelerometers, seismometers, infrasound sensors, electromagnetic sensors, chemical and radiotracer samplers, and meteorological sensors,” it adds. ”Together, these measurements will improve scientists’ understanding of the signatures produced by underground explosions and strengthen the United States’ ability to detect and characterize nuclear explosive events.”

The U.S. already maintains a U.S. Atomic Energy Detection Systems (USAEDS) network, which is overseen by the U.S. Air Force Technical Applications Center (AFTAC). USAEDS is made up of more than 3,600 sensors positioned around the world. USAEDS is also tied in with the International Monitoring System (IMS), which is managed by the organization responsible for overseeing the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT). AFTAC also supports the mission to monitor for potential nuclear testing globally using a fleet of specially configured WC-135R Constant Phoenix aircraft. In addition, those planes are used to help keep watch for unusual spikes in atmospheric radiation that could point to nuclear or radiological accidents or other incidents leading to the spread of potentially dangerous radioactive material.

With regard to the USAEDS network specifically, “once a disturbance is detected underground, underwater, in the atmosphere or in space, the event is analyzed for nuclear identification, and the findings are reported to command authorities,” according to AFTAC’s website.

As mentioned, the U.S. government has accused its Chinese counterparts of using decoupling to conceal new nuclear testing, and NNSA’s press release draws explicit attention to these allegations. At the annual Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, Switzerland, in February, Thomas DiNanno, Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security, said that China had conducted at least one such test at Lop Nur on June 22, 2020. The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) subsequently said the IMS had not detected an event matching that description at that location on that date. For its part, the Chinese government has denied the accusation.

The social media posts below include satellite imagery showing activity at Lop Nur that could point to new nuclear testing activities in recent years.

While China is a signatory to the CTBT, the country has never ratified it. The Chinese government last acknowledged a critical-level nuclear test in 1996, after which a self-imposed moratorium was put in place, at least publicly. As an aside, the United States has also signed, but never ratified, the CTBT, and has a similar self-imposed moratorium on nuclear testing since 1992. It is worth noting that the treaty does not ban so-called sub-critical testing, which involves fissile material, but does not result in a full-fledged nuclear reaction.

Last week, The Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration has been holding new talks with the Chinese government regarding various aspects of the country’s massively and rapidly expanding nuclear arsenal, including the testing allegations. That story immediately preceded a state visit by China’s President Xi Jinping to Washington, D.C., to meet with Trump.

“The discussions between American and Chinese officials have centered on measures to reduce nuclear risks and haven’t been aimed at negotiating a formal arms-control pact, an effort Beijing has sharply rebuffed in the past,” according to that report. “The Trump administration has begun to highlight the possibility of implementing new verification measures.”

“Independent experts say seismic instruments might be placed on or near test sites,” The Journal‘s story also noted. “Another possibility, which was floated during the Biden administration, is to install radiation-detection equipment at test sites.”

NNSA’s announcement about the test at the Nevada National Security Site is certainly an example of the development underway already of new means of verification that could be deployed at sites around the world.

The United States has separately accused Russia of conducting lower-yield nuclear testing in secret in the past. Russia is a signatory to the CTBT and had previously ratified it. In 2023, President Vladimir Putin revoked that ratification in line with the provisions of a law passed by the country’s parliament, or Duma.

President Trump has also floated the idea of the resumption of U.S. nuclear testing in response to Russian and Chinese activities, though other U.S. officials have downplayed the possibility of doing so. The United States is otherwise in the midst of a huge nuclear modernization effort that impacts the air, sea, and land-based legs of the deterrent triad. American authorities are also now pursuing these efforts in an environment fully unbounded by relevant arms control agreements following the sunset of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) earlier this year.

The Russian government has said it is ready to conduct new nuclear tests if the United States pursues this course of action. The last official nuclear test in Russia came in 1990 right before the fall of the Soviet Union.

“It takes nuclear expertise to detect nuclear activities and experiments like these ensure America remains unmatched in detection,” NNSA Administrator Brandon Williams said in a statement yesterday in light of the test in Nevada. “The Trump Administration has made it clear that the United States will lead from a position of strength. You cannot evade American innovation. With this experiment, we are sending a clear message: under this administration, America will never be outmatched.”

articles.title: DRDO Completes Development of Indigenous 600 HP Engine for Combat Vehicles
articles.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has finished developing a 600 horsepower engine made in India. This engine is meant for future combat vehicles. The Ministry of Defence’s annual report says the engine has been calibrated and tuned to work at full power. They also tested the durability of two prototype engines.
This development is a big step toward India relying less on imported engines for its armored fighting vehicles. It also supports India’s goal of becoming more self-sufficient in military vehicle technology. The report mentions that the engine was designed to be small, efficient, and light, which makes it a good fit for future combat vehicles. These features are crucial for modern armored vehicles because space, power-to-weight ratio, and mobility greatly affect how well they perform in battle.
The report confirms that the engine’s calibration and tuning for full power are complete. This shows the team worked to make sure the engine performs as expected under different operating conditions. A key part of the annual report is that durability tests on two prototype engines have been finished. Testing durability is vital to see how reliable an engine is when used for long periods and to find any problems before it’s put into a vehicle.
The report also states that all the project’s goals were met. While this is a good step, it doesn’t automatically mean the engine has passed all user tests or is ready for official use. A 600 HP engine could be used in various armored and specialized military vehicles, especially those that need a good balance of mobility, protection, and a compact engine design.
Future tracked combat vehicles and other heavy military platforms could use this engine. However, the annual report doesn’t specify which vehicles will be equipped with it. Developing engines in India is strategically important because powerpacks are some of the most technically challenging parts of armored vehicles. Relying on foreign suppliers can cause problems with getting spare parts, accessing technology, maintaining production, and long-term upkeep.
If an Indian-designed 600 HP engine proves reliable, performs well, and is ready for mass production, it could help boost the country’s domestic defense manufacturing capabilities.

articles.title: Microsoft makes Windows settings backup the default in 26H2
articles.text: Windows 11 26H2 is out, and Microsoft has enabled Windows settings backup by default, a move that could send administrators scrambling to opt out where they once had to opt in. The latest release hasn't made a lot of shockwaves in the community featurewise. Users with up-to-date versions of 25H2 will unlikely notice much difference – 26H2 has the same code base, delivered via an enablement package. It even has the same set of known issues, although all are now "mitigated" in one way or another. However, administrators will spot several important changes. The end-of-support clock is reset, and Microsoft has flipped some switches behind the scenes; notably, enabling Windows backup and restore (formerly Windows Backup for Organizations) by default. On by default The service, which was previously off by default, backs up a device's settings and a list of installed Microsoft Store apps. The idea is that when a user moves to a new device, a restore can happen during setup. Microsoft also listed an objective of the service as allowing "organizations to transition to a cloud-first approach for managing devices and user settings." The problem is that many organizations are prohibited from sending this data to the cloud. As a result, the default-on setting won't apply in privacy-sensitive regions such as those covered by the EU Digital Markets Act, or in sovereign and restricted environments. For many others running Windows 11 26H2, it'll now be enabled by default on eligible devices – Entra joined or Entra Hybrid joined. Unless an administrator has explicitly said no to the functionality, the act of installing the update will flip the switch, and the backups will begin. Administrators will rightly be wary of anything that switches from opt-in to opt-out, even something so apparently useful and innocuous as a backup. Why wouldn't you want your users to be able to leap to a new device with ease? That assumes their data is also in the cloud, of course, since this only backs up settings and a list of Windows apps. Backing up data is something else entirely. That is the real issue with the change. The release of Windows 11 26H2 isn't particularly exciting in itself, but flipping a long-standing opt-in to opt-out as part of it is likely to set more than a few nerves jangling. ®

articles.title: Build the right AI factory for your needs: partner for success
articles.text: AI ambition is easy to describe - using data and models to improve decisions, automate work, accelerate discovery, or create new services. Delivering those outcomes is harder and takes a significant amount of experience to be successful. Training a frontier model, fine-tuning an industry model, running high-volume inference and supporting agentic AI place different demands on infrastructure, processes and people. Implementing AI may include a single-purpose turnkey configuration that will accommodate one line of business, or the business may demand a more strategic approach to capitalize on the economies of scale and create AI as a multi-tenant service, designed to accommodate the multitude of mainstream business requirements. That is the value of an AI factory, bringing the complete AI lifecycle together so a cost-effective infrastructure can be designed around the mission, scaled with demand, secured as needed and operated as a dependable source of intelligence. The AI factory is designed to deliver the capacity, performance, utilization and business value customers expect. From AI workload to business outcome An AI factory is an integrated solution for data ingestion, model development, training, fine-tuning, inference, monitoring and continuous improvement. Its purpose is to turn data into intelligence repeatedly and efficiently—whether that intelligence supports a clinician, an engineer, a researcher, a public service or an enterprise application. Achieving that goal requires more than choosing an accelerated processor. Compute must match the business model and expected workloads. Networking and data pipelines must keep accelerators supplied. Storage must support the volume and velocity of data. Software must provision resources and orchestrate jobs. Security, governance and multi-tenancy must reflect who will use the environment and what data they can access. Power and cooling must support the system’s density today and as it grows. “Without proper architecture, governance and operational expertise, organizations can't safely leverage their data, take AI into core processes, or turn innovation into durable competitive advantage,” says Thierry Pienaar, HPE Fellow, Vice President and CTO for HPC and AI Sales. “Customers are realizing the fact that to derive value to its utmost extent they need an end-to-end infrastructure that's purpose-designed and purpose-built for AI.” Choice starts with the workload The HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA portfolio brings together NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking and AI software with HPE infrastructure, software, services and expertise at deploying complex systems. Rather than forcing every customer into a single configuration, the portfolio provides three paths for different ambitions, operating models and requirements. ● HPE Private Cloud AI, the turnkey AI factory solution, is an enterprise-ready, on-premises AI platform for running fine tuning, RAG & inferencing workload environments that need up to 256 GPUs. ● HPE AI Factory at-scale supports model builders, service providers and large enterprises that operate across many users, workloads and GPU resources (using 100s to 10s of thousands of GPUs) with centralized control, operational visibility, and multi-tenancy over the entire AI lifecycle ● HPE Sovereign AI Factory is an HPE AI factory at-scale that adds a deep level of operational control, data security and residency, sovereign management (including optional air-gapped configurations), and built-in compliance frameworks. It is designed for large enterprises, and any other organizations with sensitive information that require strict control and compliance across data, infrastructure, models and operations within defined legal, regulatory or geographic boundaries. Each option starts with the same principle: define the workloads and desired outcomes first, then select the right technologies to support them and finally identify the required resources needed to implement such an infrastructure. A hospital deploying clinical assistants will make different choices from a service provider offering GPU capacity, a manufacturer training vision models or a government operating sensitive national workloads. The HPE AI Factory model gives each a way to build for its mission without losing sight of performance, control or future growth – and HPE partners with these organizations to dramatically increase the likelihood of success. Operate the environment as one system As the use of AI expands across an organization, the operational challenges mature. Multiple teams may need different resource profiles, application stacks, service levels and data boundaries. Platform teams need to see utilization, allocate capacity, apply policy and understand consumption without creating a separate infrastructure island for every workload. The management of these differences make time-to-production an increasingly useful way to think about AI infrastructure: How quickly can an organization cost effectively move from investment vision to an operational environment generating useful intelligence? Many enterprises initially try to answer that question by extending their existing IT expertise. But building a DIY production AI environment from individual components requires skill sets that many enterprise IT organizations have never needed or required at this scale. A poorly implemented AI system may technically operate while still failing economically or operationally. GPUs can sit underutilized. Data pipelines can create bottlenecks. Cooling or power constraints can limit operation and/or expansion. Security policies can prevent sensitive data and workloads from being included. Separate less understood management systems can make AI factory infrastructure difficult to operate. "The HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA portfolio gives enterprises a range of AI solutions co-developed with NVIDIA, backed by HPE’s engineering expertise and technical capabilities to design an AI factory around their specific needs and optimize it for performance at scale." That control helps customers align capacity with workload priorities while keeping the environment easier to manage as it grows. For others, it means controlling who can access systems, where workloads run, how models are governed, and which local laws apply.” HPE and NVIDIA engineer for the complete outcome HPE and NVIDIA co-engineer AI factory solutions to reduce the integration work required to deploy and operate a high efficiency enterprise AI environment. By combining NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking, and AI software with HPE infrastructure, cloud operations, services, and support, the joint solution helps data scientists and developers spend more time building and improving AI applications while platform teams maintain operational production and control. NVIDIA provides accelerated computing platforms, networking, and the NVIDIA AI Enterprise software suite to power modern training, fine-tuning, inference, and agentic workloads. HPE contributes its expertise in enterprise systems engineering, high-performance computing, management and observability software, services, global support, financing, and years of experience in the power and cooling requirements of dense computing environments. Together, the companies can optimize AI computing solutions beyond any single component. articles.title: Embraer’s C-390M and Future Co-Development of 40-Ton Transporters with India
articles.text:
The Indian Air Force (IAF) is seeking to modernize its transport aircraft fleet which currently consists of Soviet-era Antonov An-32 and Ilyushin Il-76 aircraft to be replaced by 2035 and complement its Boeing C-17 Globemaster IIIs aircraft. Embraer has positioned itself as a major player to provide its C-390M Millennium transport aircraft for the IAF’s Medium Transport Aircraft (MTA) program.
Besides proposing its C-390M transport aircraft to the IAF, Embraer has also shown its willingness to co-develop 40-ton payload transport aircraft with India’s public and private companies for a niche market of versatile, high capacity transport aircraft. Such a venture can provide India with cutting-edge aerospace technologies and satisfy the IAF’s requirements under the Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative.
Embraer’s C-390M Millennium is a twin-engine jet-powered military transport aircraft with a payload capacity of 26 tons. It is more versatile and cost-effective than the C-130J Super Hercules (20 tons) and compares to the A400M Atlas (37 tons) in terms of its payload capacity. Its multi-role capabilities include transporting troops and cargo, providing medical support, aerial refueling, search and rescue, maritime patrol and strike operations after modifications. Additionally, it has a high cruising speed of Mach 0.8, a low-pressure landing gear enabling landing on primitive runways, and a state-of-the-art cargo-handling system. The C-390M Millennium would be perfect for the IAF’s requirement for 40-80 aircraft to replace its aging fleet of An-32 and Il-76 transport aircraft.
Embraer has boosted its prospects of selling the C-390Ms to the IAF by signing an MoU with Mahindra Defence Systems in February 2024 to manufacture the aircraft in India and establish the country as a regional aircraft manufacturing hub. This cooperation aims to achieve self-reliance in defense production under the Make in India program and generate significant technology transfer and supply chains to provide spares which would ensure at least a 90% serviceability rate of the aircraft compared to only 50% currently for the IAF’s Soviet-era aircraft.
The C-390M’s multi-role capabilities are a great advantage over its competitors. Embraer has proposed modifying the C-390M for various secondary roles such as Airborne Early Warning (AEW), maritime patrol, aerial refueling, and Intelligence Surveillance Target Acquisition and Reconnaissance (ISTAR). It can also be modified to carry air-to-surface missiles or torpedoes; for instance, India has the Rudram-II missile (800 kg), or anti-ship missiles for maritime patrol roles. The C-390M can carry other combat-related payloads and systems, such as air-launched drones or the Nirbhay cruise missile (1,500 km range). Thus, the C-390M can provide the IAF with an option to fulfill its transport needs and supplement its strike roles with minimal investment in dedicated bomber aircraft.
Embraer’s most ambitious proposal is to co-develop a larger and more capable transport aircraft with a 40-ton payload capacity with India’s public and private companies for a niche market. It fits in with India’s plans to develop indigenous defense technologies. While Embraer has shown its willingness to co-develop the aircraft, details regarding the type of companies to participate in the venture are yet to emerge. Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and private companies such as Mahindra or Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL) may be involved in the venture. The proposed aircraft would have a payload capacity between the C-390M Millennium (26 tons) and the C-17 Globemaster III (77.5 tons). The IAF has acquired 11 C-17 aircraft compared to the 31 C-17s ordered by the Pakistan Air Force (PAF). Thus, a 40-ton aircraft would be a good fit for the IAF.
The IAF has a significant requirement for transport aircraft as its fleet of Soviet-era aircraft is outdated and ill-suited for the modern battlefield as well as its own strategic airlift requirements. The An-32 has a payload capacity of 6.7 tons while the Il-76 has a payload capacity of 48 tons but both aircraft have been plagued by maintenance issues and low serviceability rates. The C-17s have been reliable but there are only 11 aircraft in the IAF’s inventory. The IAF requires more aircraft to meet its requirements, especially considering the 2020 Galwan standoff when the IAF flew more than 68,000 troops, 90 tanks, and 300 infantry fighting vehicles to J&K. The C-17s and a 40-ton transport aircraft would be able to provide the IAF with strategic airlift capabilities during such crises. Moreover, the IAF often undertakes Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) operations or other missions that require airlift capabilities that the C-17s or the C-390M cannot fulfill.
The co-development of a 40-ton transport aircraft with India’s public and private companies could prove to be a great opportunity for Embraer as it would gain access to a lucrative market while increasing its profits tremendously. However, such a venture would be capital and time-intensive, and there are doubts as to whether Embraer has the resources to commit to the endeavor. Secondly, the IAF’s MTA tender has not yet been finalized; other competitors such as the C-130J Super Hercules and the A400M Atlas are in the running for the deal, and there is no certain date as to when a final decision will be reached by the IAF. Lastly, integrating indigenous Indian systems, such as DRDO radars or missiles, will involve extensive tests to ensure compatibility.

articles.title: Microsoft catches hackers exploiting Zimbra bug before disclosure
articles.text: Attackers were poking at a critical Zimbra mail server bug weeks before it was publicly disclosed, and then moved on to steal credentials, raid mailboxes, and take deeper control of compromised systems. Microsoft Threat Intelligence said it tracked exploitation of CVE-2026-73570, an unauthenticated command injection vulnerability in Zimbra Collaboration Suite that gives attackers a potentially easy route into exposed mail servers. No stolen password or unfortunate employee clicking a dodgy link is required. An attacker can send a specially crafted email to a vulnerable internet-facing server and potentially run commands, though Redmond notes the flaw affects only servers running Zimbra's optional SNMP monitoring package with notifications enabled. Zimbra fixed the flaw in version 10.1.20 on July 20, but CVE-2026-73570 wasn't publicly disclosed until August 13. Between July 28 and August 7, Redmond spotted two different scanning tools probing the same part of Zimbra later used in attacks. At first, the activity appears to have focused on finding vulnerable servers and testing the flaw. The attackers used a collection of common network utilities to make vulnerable systems call back to infrastructure they controlled, confirming they could execute commands. Once they found servers that played ball, things got messier. Microsoft's investigation found attackers deploying web shells and reverse shells, escalating their privileges, installing tools for persistent remote access, and running malicious code directly in memory. Some even tidied up after themselves. Microsoft said attackers temporarily changed permissions on public directories to plant web shells, then restored the original settings afterward in an apparent attempt to make their meddling harder to spot. The intruders also explored the wider Zimbra environments they landed in, identifying other mail servers and looking for trusted connections they could use to move between them. In some cases, existing SSH relationships between Zimbra systems gave them a route to neighboring servers. On at least one compromised machine, attackers turned their initial foothold into root access. They then set things up to keep running commands with the highest privileges without needing a password. Mailboxes were, unsurprisingly, also on the shopping list. Microsoft said attackers hunted for Zimbra credentials and authentication secrets that could potentially be used to access user accounts. One malicious tool it uncovered was built specifically to extract service account credentials and pull mailbox information from Zimbra's databases. In another incident, attackers bundled recent mailbox backups into an archive and tried to ship the haul to Azure Blob Storage using Microsoft's own AzCopy utility. Microsoft said it couldn't confirm from the evidence available whether the transfer actually succeeded. The company saw affected organizations across multiple regions and industries, with the attacks ranging from automated exploitation to more deliberate hands-on-keyboard activity. It hasn't attributed the activity to a particular crew. Admins running versions earlier than Zimbra 10.1.20 should update to 10.1.20 or later, while those unable to patch can reduce their exposure by removing the optional SNMP package or disabling SNMP notifications. Attackers, meanwhile, appear to have gotten there early, with Microsoft spotting probes for the flaw more than two weeks before it was publicly disclosed. ®

India’s home-grown Akash surface-to-air missiles have been purchased by two more nations apart from Armenia, revealed Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh. India has supplied Akash missiles to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, he added.
This is a major confirmation of what ex-DRDO chief Dr Samir V. Kamat had hinted at in the media last year. Singh’s comments were the first public confirmation from the Defence Ministry about the sale. Earlier reports carried by defence analysts from the region noted that it had not been easy to confirm the sales since none of the two nations had officially shared the information.
Apart from Armenia, there was no other publicly known buyer of India’s air defence system till this week. Reuters had, in fact, reported in 2025 that Armenia had signed a $230-million deal for the acquisition of the Akash system. According to that report, the range of the missile was 25 km. Officially, on the DRDO website, the Akash system states that they have supplied the missile defence system to foreign countries.
It also says that Bharat Dynamics and Bharat Electronics have trained personnel from friendly countries. It further mentions that the first battery/firing unit of the Akash system has been flagged off for delivery, though the countries aren’t named. Singh noted that the production of Akash missiles had “stabilised.” He added that India continues to receive requests for more missiles.
Meanwhile, Rajesh Kumar Singh said, “Tajikistan and Turkmenistan open a new dimension for India in the region.” Both these nations are locked in a strategic location, which has been a matter of security concern for them. The Akash system offers a mobile medium-range defence against aircraft and missiles.

MI5 warns UK academics their research may have helped Chinese spies
articles.text: MI5 has warned that more than 100 UK-linked academics contributed to research projects allegedly funded to improve China's spying capabilities. The Security Service issued an unusually public espionage alert this week naming the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), also translated as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT). MI5 says the organization has "very strong ties" to China's Ministry of State Security (MSS), the country's civilian intelligence agency. According to MI5, CGTRI's "primary purpose" is to fund academic research that directly improves the MSS's technical espionage capabilities. More than 100 UK-linked academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects involving AI, cybersecurity, covert communications, and steganography, the agency said. Some may not have known who was ultimately financing the work. "This activity supports MSS espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security," MI5 said. MI5 isn't accusing all of the academics involved of knowingly helping Chinese intelligence. Its alert acknowledges that many institutions and individuals likely dealt with CGTRI "in good faith" because of what it describes as the organization's "obfuscated links" to the MSS. MI5 "strongly advised" UK universities to review immediately any current or planned collaboration with CGTRI and ensure that the MSS derives no further benefit from British research. Academics working with Chinese institutions are also being told to establish who is ultimately funding the research and make sure CGTRI isn't involved. Researchers may also want to brush up on the National Security Act 2023. MI5 specifically highlighted two offenses: assisting a foreign intelligence service under section 3 and obtaining a material benefit from one under section 17. Under section 3, a person can commit an offense if their conduct is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service with UK-related activities and they know, or "ought reasonably to know," that it is likely to do so. Section 17 separately covers accepting or retaining a material benefit when the recipient knows, or ought reasonably to know, that it came from a foreign intelligence service. Legitimate payment for lawful goods or services is excluded. Having publicly identified CGTRI's alleged links to Chinese intelligence, MI5 warned that any institution or researcher continuing to conduct work funded by the organization should seek independent legal advice. In other words, MI5 has put universities on notice: not knowing who was really behind the research money may have been understandable yesterday, but it is a considerably trickier argument today. ®
